metadata.file_name: 26. Bencomo-Mesa et al. (2025). Inequality of Opportunity in Education in Spanish Regions: A Machine Learning Approach.pdf
metadata.title: Inequality of Opportunity in Education in Spanish Regions: A Machine Learning Approach

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for Spain with an expanded sample designed to be regionally representative across all Spanish regions. The analytic task is to estimate inequality of opportunity (IOpE) using conditional inference trees (CIT) and conditional inference forests (CIF) with bootstrapping and averaging across the 10 PISA plausible values for achievement in science. The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights in the ML estimation stage; given the ML algorithms used (CIT/CIF) and the absence of explicit weight-variable references, weighting is likely not incorporated in the model fitting. For comparability across regions, the authors standardize the ML tuning parameters (common alpha, number of trees, and mtry) and compute confidence intervals via bootstrapping rather than via replicate-weight variance estimation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper discusses that CIT/CIF importance calculations can handle missing values (via the conditional inference framework), but it does not specify the exact missing-data rule used for the analytic sample (e.g., surrogate splits settings beyond maxsurrogate=3, whether cases are listwise-deleted, or how missingness is treated within each bootstrap and across plausible values). This is a reporting gap because IOpE estimates and circumstance importance can be sensitive to how missing covariates are handled, especially when tuning tree depth and split criteria.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 for Spain with regionally representative coverage of all Spanish regions; the IOpE estimation is performed for science achievement and then averaged across the 10 PISA plausible values. The ML tuning and estimation are carried out under three scenarios (baseline, unrestricted, parameter tuning), with the preferred CIF using common tuning parameters across regions (alpha=0.80, M=5, N=150). For CIT, alpha is tuned via cross-validation; for CIF, alpha and M are tuned using out-of-bag MSE with N fixed at 150. The methodology notes the presence of missing values in explanatory variables and uses surrogate splits (maxsurrogate=3) to address missingness in tree construction.

main_findings.target_variable: Inequality of opportunity in science achievement (IOpE; variance share explained by circumstances)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Conditional Inference Forest (CIF, parameter tuning: alpha=0.80, M=5, N=150) — average IOpE about 43% vs 20% from traditional OLS-linear approach (Sicilia et al., 2022); region range (preferred ML, science): 40.5% to 48.7% with Murcia, Extremadura, and Cataluña highest; Castilla-La Mancha and País Vasco lowest. Confidence intervals obtained via bootstrapping (200 bootstraps).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Science data for Spain’s regions, the study leveraged home cultural environment (Number of books at home) and parental socioeconomic circumstances (Mother occupation and Father occupation), along with Cultural possessions index and Household wealth index, to estimate the IOpE distribution via conditional inference forests, finding that CIF-based IOpE is more than twice the traditional OLS-linear estimates on average (43% vs 20%). This indicates that conventional regression-based approaches likely understate inequality of opportunity in Spanish regions, implying that regional equity diagnostics and targeted support policies should be informed by ML-based, bias-robust IOpE measurement rather than relying solely on parametric R²-style estimates.

data.outcome_summary: The paper estimates inequality of opportunity in educational achievement (IOpE) for Spanish regions using PISA 2018 microdata, focusing on science achievement for students aged 15–16. The authors model the share of achievement variance explained by circumstances beyond students’ control using conditional inference trees (CIT) and conditional inference forests (CIF), with CIF selected under a parameter-tuning scenario (alpha=0.80, M=5, N=150) to balance downward and upward bias. IOpE from CIF is about twice the traditional OLS-linear benchmark (on average 43% vs 20%), with preferred ML estimates ranging roughly from 40.5% to 48.7% across regions; Murcia, Extremadura, and Cataluña are highest, while Castilla-La Mancha and País Vasco are lowest. The study averages results across the 10 PISA plausible values for science and uses bootstrapping (200 resamples) to form confidence intervals. A key limitation is that the manuscript does not clearly report how PISA sampling/replicate weights are incorporated in the ML estimation, and missing-data handling is only partially specified (surrogate splits are mentioned), which may affect the stability of IOpE and circumstance importance.
